head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Guards against counting a value twice within the same list
`Counter(x for lst in nums for x in set(lst))`
Number of lists that contain each value
Nested generator: outer loop over lists, inner over each list's distinct values
The value is in every list

blocks.h: Why Counter over lists and not pairwise set intersection?
p: Intersecting sets one after another also works (`set.intersection(*map(set, nums))`). The Counter version makes the 'in every list' rule explicit: a value present in all lists is counted exactly len(nums) times, because each list contributes at most once per value.

bullets: Time: O(N log N), where N is the total number of elements (the sort of the result).

2248.takeaway: Count in how many lists each value occurs (deduplicating within a list); keep those counted in all lists.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Independent sorted lists of starts and ends
Flowers that started on or before day p
Includes flowers starting exactly on p
Flowers that ended strictly before day p
A flower ending on day p is still in bloom, so `bisect_left` (excluding ends equal to p)
Flowers in bloom on day p

blocks.h: Why can starts and ends be sorted separately?
p: The answer only needs two counts: how many flowers have started, and how many have finished. Pairing each start with its end doesn't matter, because every finished flower has also started (its start ≤ its end < p). Subtracting the counts therefore gives the flowers that started but have not ended.

2251.takeaway: Count flowers started (bisect_right on sorted starts) minus flowers ended (bisect_left on sorted ends).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of texts for the first i key presses
Max presses per letter on this key
The block of presses is all the same key
A letter can only come from a run of identical digits
Block length j…i is at most `limit`
Last letter uses presses j…i, the rest forms any message

blocks.h: Why does the run of equal digits matter?
p: One letter is a block of 1 to `limit` identical digits. For each position i the code tries every block length ending at i (while the digits stay equal) and adds the number of ways to type the earlier part. The three 2s give 4 ways (`aaa`, `ab`, `ba`, `c`) and the two 3s give 2 (`dd`, `e`), so 4 × 2 = 8.

bullets: Time: O(n) (each position tries at most 4 block lengths).

2266.takeaway: DP over key presses: the last letter takes 1 to 3 (or 4) identical presses; add the counts of the shorter prefixes.

p: `[16,17,71,62,12,24,14]` → 4 (bits 2, 3 and 4 each have 4 numbers with that bit set):

blocks.h: Why does the answer reduce to one bit?
p: A group has bitwise AND > 0 exactly when some bit is set in every member. So a group works if all its members share a common set bit, and the largest group for a bit b consists of ALL numbers with bit b set. The best answer is the largest such count over all bits.

2275.takeaway: A group has AND > 0 iff all members share a set bit: count numbers per bit and take the maximum.

Stack in reverse order, so popping gives the next character to the right
Appends each character of the string

p: Sequence of calls (`left`/`right` shown as text; `right` is shown in reading order):

Every operation happens at the cursor: inserting and deleting at the end of `left`, moving the cursor by popping from one stack and pushing onto the other. Each operation costs time proportional to the characters involved (k), not the whole text length, which a plain string with an index would pay on every insertion in the middle.

bullets: Time: O(k) per call for k characters moved/deleted (inserting text costs O(len(text)); returning the last 10 characters is O(10)).

2296.takeaway: Two stacks around the cursor: edits happen at the end of the left stack and cursor moves shift characters between the stacks.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Score of the window is too large
Score only decreases when elements are removed (values are positive)
Count all valid subarrays ENDING at r
Every shorter window ending at r also has a smaller score

blocks.h: Why does the sliding window work?
p: All numbers are positive, so removing an element from the left decreases both the sum and the length, hence the score. That monotonicity means that for each right end, the valid left ends form a contiguous range, and as `r` grows the smallest valid `left` never moves backwards. Every start from `left` to `r` gives a valid subarray: that is `r - left + 1` of them.

bullets: Time: O(n): `left` and `r` each move forward at most n times.

2302.takeaway: Sliding window on sum × length (monotone for positive numbers): count r − left + 1 valid subarrays per right end.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Scan from the least significant bit
Position from the right gives the bit's weight 1, 2, 4, …
They can always be taken (leading zeros are allowed)
Taking this 1 keeps the value within k
Greedy: prefer the cheapest ones (rightmost = smallest weight)
Once weight > k no further 1 can fit; capping avoids huge integers

blocks.h: Why take all zeros and the smallest ones?
p: A zero costs nothing in value, so keeping them all is free. Each 1 adds its weight, so to keep as many as possible choose those with the smallest weights, which are the rightmost ones (weights grow to the left). Scanning from the right and taking a 1 whenever it still fits does exactly this.

2311.takeaway: Greedy from the right: keep every 0, and keep a 1 only while the running value (sum of weights) stays at most k.

Condition for x to divide everything in numsDivide
Smallest valid x, or `None` if the generator is empty
Those must all be deleted so that `best` becomes the smallest

head: Step
Value
rows: values in nums that divide g

p: x divides every number in a list exactly when it divides their gcd, so one gcd replaces m divisibility tests per candidate. The smallest valid x in `nums` is the cheapest target: all numbers smaller than it must be removed (they are not valid divisors, or removing them is necessary for x to be the minimum), while larger ones can stay.

2344.takeaway: Reduce numsDivide to its gcd; the target is the smallest nums value dividing it, and the answer counts the smaller elements.

How many times each rank occurs
The largest count identifies pairs and triples
3 or more → Three of a Kind; 2 → Pair
Flush beats the others as the problem defines the order

blocks.h: Why three or more counts as 'Three of a Kind'?
p: With five cards a rank can appear up to 5 times, and the problem says three (or more) of the same rank is 'Three of a Kind'. Checking `m >= 3` handles four or five of a kind without extra branches.

2347.takeaway: Check suits with a set, then use the highest rank multiplicity from a Counter.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Negated rating puts the highest rating on top; ties compare the food name alphabetically
Lazy deletion: updating inside a heap would cost O(n)
Discard entries whose rating is outdated
Stale entries are cleaned only when they reach the top
Highest rating, alphabetically first on ties

p: foods kimchi (korean, 9), miso (japanese, 12), sushi (japanese, 8), moussaka (greek, 15), ramen (japanese, 14), bulgogi (korean, 7):

Heaps do not support efficient removal or update of an arbitrary item. Instead, every rating change pushes a fresh `(−new rating, food)` entry, and old entries remain until they surface at the top, where they are recognised as stale by comparing with the current rating in `self.rating`. Each entry is popped at most once, so the cost is O(log n) amortised. When two foods tie at 16 (ramen and sushi), the tuple comparison puts the alphabetically smaller name first.

bullets: Time: O(log n) amortised per call.

2353.takeaway: Per-cuisine heaps with lazy deletion: push a new entry on each update and discard outdated tops when querying.

head: Task
Decision
Day done
rows: too soon (last on day 1) → jump to day 5
too soon (last on day 5) → jump to day 9

blocks.h: Why a jump and not simulating each waiting day?
p: Waiting means doing nothing until the earliest allowed day. Computing that day directly (`last + space + 1`) avoids looping over idle days, which could be up to 10⁹ long. Because tasks must run in order, a later task can't fill the idle days.

2365.takeaway: Hash map of last-done day per type; if too soon, jump straight to last + space + 1.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of zeros to the left
Each 1 must pass every zero before it, one step per second at best
Time at which the previous 1 finished moving
The previous 1 blocks the next one
This 1 needs at least `zeros` seconds (one per zero) and can't be earlier than one second after the previous 1
Ignore 1s with no zero before them

blocks.h: Why is the formula max(t + 1, zeros)?
p: Each 1 wants to move left past every zero before it: that takes at least `zeros` seconds. But a 1 can't overtake the previous 1, and a 1 can only start to move after the one in front has moved away, so it finishes at least one second after the previous 1: `t + 1`. The later of the two lower bounds is the finishing time, and the last 1's time is the answer.

2380.takeaway: Pipeline timing: each 1 finishes at max(previous 1's time + 1, number of zeros before it).

Prefix sums of the sorted list
`pre[i]` = sum of the i+1 smallest numbers
Number of prefix sums that are ≤ q
The size of the largest prefix with sum ≤ q

p: To fit as many numbers as possible under a sum limit, pick the smallest ones. The prefix sums of the sorted array are increasing, so `bisect_right` finds how many fit by binary search. The original order doesn't matter since a subsequence is judged by its sum, not by position.

2389.takeaway: Sort, build prefix sums, and bisect_right each query to count how many smallest numbers fit.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Bitwise OR of all numbers in the window
Since the numbers have disjoint bits, the OR equals their XOR and also their sum
Bits that the new number shares with the window
XOR undoes an OR when the bits are disjoint

blocks.h: Why check the OR instead of every pair?
p: All pairs in the window have AND 0 exactly when no bit appears in two numbers, i.e. the bit sets are pairwise disjoint. Keeping the OR of the window and testing `used & x` finds a conflict in O(1) instead of comparing x with each member. XOR removal is valid because disjoint sets mean each bit belongs to exactly one number.

2401.takeaway: Sliding window whose elements have pairwise disjoint bits: keep their OR and shrink while the new number overlaps it.

Tuple key: negated count sorts larger counts first, then the value
Guard before calling `min` on an empty dict (which would raise)

blocks.h: Why `min` with a tuple key instead of sorting?
p: Only the best element is needed. `min` with a key scans once (O(k)) rather than sorting (O(k log k)). The key `(-count, value)` encodes both rules: larger counts win, and among equal counts the smaller value wins.

2404.takeaway: Count the even numbers; take the min by the key (−count, value).

p: If the ends differ, the smaller end can never become equal to the larger end without being merged with its neighbour (merging the larger one would only make it bigger and the gap wider). Greedily merging the smaller side is both necessary and sufficient, and each merge reduces the problem by one element.

2422.takeaway: Two pointers: when the ends differ, merge the smaller end into its neighbour; equal ends move inward.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Best tastiness using at most `a` money and at most `c` coupons
`for a in range(maxAmount, -1, -1)`, `for c in range(maxCoupons, -1, -1)`
Each fruit is used at most once: reads of smaller `a`/`c` still hold the previous fruit's values
Buy with a coupon: half price rounded down, one coupon
Best of skip / buy / buy with coupon

p: prices `[10,20,20]`, tastiness `[5,8,8]`, `maxAmount = 20`, `maxCoupons = 1` → 13 (buy the first fruit at 10 and the second with a coupon at 10: 5 + 8). Selected cells after each fruit:

blocks.h: Why iterate downward in both dimensions?
p: `dp[a][c]` is updated in place using cells with smaller `a` or `c` (dp[a−p][c] and dp[a−p//2][c−1]). Processing in decreasing order means those cells still hold the values from BEFORE the current fruit, so the fruit can't be bought twice. This is the same trick as the 1-D 0/1 knapsack, with a second dimension for coupons.

2431.takeaway: Knapsack with two budgets: dp over (money, coupons), iterating both downward so each fruit is used once; a coupon halves the price.

p: `'bac'` → `abc`:

The paper wants the smallest string. If the top of t is at most every letter still to come, writing it now can't be worse than waiting. If a strictly smaller letter is still in s, we must keep moving characters until that smaller letter appears and can be written first. The comparison `<=` writes equal letters immediately, which is also never worse.

bullets: Time: O(n + 26 n) ≈ O(n): `mn` only moves forward (at most 26 steps total).

2434.takeaway: Monotonic-stack greedy: write the stack's top whenever it is not larger than the smallest letter still unread.

p: Two intervals do NOT overlap only if one ends before the other starts. Negating that: `start1 <= end2 and start2 <= end1`. Because the events are inclusive (touching at 02:00 counts), the comparisons use `<=`, which is why the first example is a conflict.

2446.takeaway: Convert HH:MM to minutes; closed intervals overlap iff start1 ≤ end2 and start2 ≤ end1.
